opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a carefully planned decision at the time. I was finishing undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, in the ACM class, and I had a PhD offer from CUHK, which was a very good option. But I felt I hadn't really seen the bigger picture yet. A lot of the most exciting work in systems, programming languages, and machine learning was happening in the US, and I wanted to be closer to it, to see how people there did research and what kinds of problems they cared about.

A PhD is a five- or six-year commitment, and I wasn't sure I'd found the direction I wanted to spend those years on. A master's at Columbia felt like a way to explore first: take different courses, work with different professors, try things without locking myself in too early. It also kept the door open to applying to US PhD programs later with stronger research experience and a clearer sense of what I wanted.

So it was a bit of a gamble. Giving up a guaranteed PhD offer for a master's, which you pay for yourself and which has no guaranteed next step, was a little scary. But I think I cared more about finding the right direction than about taking the safe path. Looking back, that exploration period was really important. It's a big part of how I ended up at Stanford and eventually working on the things I do now.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was less of a grand plan and more of a gut feeling. I had the PhD offer from CUHK, and on paper it made total sense. But at the time, I wasn't sure I actually wanted to commit five years to research. I'd done an undergrad at Peking University, I'd done some research, but I didn't feel like I'd seen enough of the world to say, "yes, this is the one problem I want to spend half a decade on."

A master's felt like a lower-cost way to figure that out. Columbia put me in New York, which meant exposure to a lot of different people, different industry options, different research groups, all at once. I could take courses, try internships, talk to professors, and see what actually excited me instead of guessing.

There was also a very practical side. At that point I didn't have a strong enough profile to get directly into the top US PhD programs I was most interested in. The master's was a bridge. It gave me time to build up research experience and connections, and that's actually what eventually led me to Stanford for my PhD.

So looking back, it was partly uncertainty, partly strategy. I gave up something that seemed safe in exchange for more optionality, and in my case it worked out. But I'll admit, at the time it felt a bit risky, and my parents definitely had questions.
